#8295. 4 Speed Records and Free Solos That Went Down in the Last 2 Weeks

Becca Droz (left) and Kate Kelleghan (right) set a new female speed record on the classic 'Naked Edge' in Boulder's Eldorado Canyon on October 26. (Photo: Jon and Jess Glassberg / Courtesy COROS)

Maybe it’s the erratic weather pressures of El Niño, or perhaps there’s just a particularly competitive spirit in the air right now. In the past two weeks, several climbers have broken records, made improbable repeats, and soloed terrain that would make many of us squirm.

Last week, we looked into the culture of free solo speed climbing in Boulder, Colorado, speaking with several athletes about the risks and influences they carry in their high-stakes sport. On the heels of this deep dive, two of the athletes who spoke to us went on to break additional records of their own within the past few days. This includes a new FKT on Half Dome and a fresh women’s speed record on Eldorado’s most famous route.

More broadly, we’ve seen a few historic achievements in the past couple weeks by free soloists and speed athletes alike. Here are four record-breakers we’ve been watching lately, in chronological order.

Just a few weeks ago, Alex Honnold told Adrian Ballinger that he thought someone would likely repeat his free solo of El Capitan before anyone dared to repeat his insanely hard linkup of peaks and scrambles in Red Rock. Back in 2022, he dubbed that linkup the Honnold Ultimate Red Rock Traverse (aka the HURT).

Honnold will have to eat his words, because on October 19, Nevada climbing guide Nik Mirhashemi put down the world’s second HURT, with slight modifications. Friends have been calling his revised route the NURT: Nik’s Ultimate Red Rock Traverse.

For the NURT, the 36-year-old skipped four non-technical summits, including Goodman, Buffalo Wall, Sandstone North, and Limestone North. Instead he traversed from White Rock Peak to ascend the seven-pitch Frigid Air Buttress (5.9+; 800ft). He then continued to the top of Icebox Peak. “Basically, I had to choose between adding Frigid Air or sticking with the OG route, where those nontechnical peaks are,” Mirhashemi said. “I didn’t want to skip Frigid Air as it is quite classic.” He also called the section he swapped in one of the traverse’s “routefinding cruxes.”

Despite the variations, Mirhashemi doesn’t think there’s a significant difference in effort level. He said that though his traverse is slightly shorter, he added more technical terrain, making the difference essentially a wash. “Nice to add a little personal flair to these things I suppose,” Mirhashemi said.

“I wanted to try the HURT for similar reasons to Alex,” Mirhashemi told Climbing. “Super long days of soloing moderate terrain is one of my favorite things to do. I’ve been coming out to Red Rock for many years and just moved here a year ago. I’m always looking for new ways to challenge myself and it just made sense as a goal right in my backyard.”

Last spring, Mirhashemi made his first HURT attempt, then completed several “scoping missions”  to prepare for his fall go. “I was never sure if I could pull it off,” he said. “Stoked it’s not haunting me anymore!”

Kate Kelleghan has been busy breaking her own record again, shaving minutes and seconds off the female fastest known time on The Naked Edge (5.11b), a classic multi-pitch in Colorado’s Eldorado Canyon.

Kelleghan, along with her French partner Laura Pineau, already held the record for the route’s women’s speed record of 37 minutes and eight seconds, which was 32 seconds faster than Kelleghan’s previous go in 2021 with Becca Droz, a Boulder-based climbing guide.

In late October, Kelleghan began working the route again with Droz. And on October 26, the athletes set a new record of 36 minutes, 26 seconds, shaving 42 seconds off the previous record.

“Becca and I were the team that started the women’s record, so taking it back together feels full circle for our friendship and our community,” Kelleghan said. Droz added that being able to track splits, as well as time out the approach, actual climb, and descent with their COROS watches “was a game changer”; both women are COROS athletes.

The men’s record is held by John Ebers and Ben Wilbur at 24 minutes and 14 seconds.

Just a couple months after smashing the speed record on the First Flatiron in Boulder, 32-year-old American climber Michael Reese established a fastest known time on Yosemite’s Half Dome on October 28. In so doing, he broke an 11-year FKT set by the late Dean Potter. Reese climbed the 2,000-foot batholith from the Mist Trailhead to its summit in 1 hour, 12 minutes, and 58 seconds. He followed Potter’s original line up Grizzly Gully, then free soloed Snake Dike (5.7 R; 800ft). He broke Potter’s previous record set on May 3, 2015 by about six minutes.

A few days after his Half Dome lap, our reporter Holly Chen, who also reported on his Flatiron speed record, caught up with Reese.

“In 2021, one of Dean Potter’s good friends told me about this as a potential record to try. He became one of my main climbing partners,” Reese told Chen. Since then, Reese has made 16 attempts and several scouting missions before his record-breaking attempt in late October.

“Records are made to be broken. I’m not gonna be surprised if it’s broken one day,” Reese said.

In the second-hardest free solo by a woman, Aleksandra “Ola” Taistra climbed a seven-pitch, 720-foot route in Sardinia, Italy on October 29. The line in question is Margarites (7a+/5.12a) up the limestone cliffs of Monte Oddeu. Established in 1998 by Andrea Calvo and Lorenzo Nadali, the route has become one of Sardinia’s “most sought-after lines,” according to Taistra. It includes a bouldery 7a+/5.12a crux pitch high off the deck; two 7a/5.11d pitches; and four additional pitches graded 6c+/5.11c, 6b+/5.11a, 6a+/5.10c, and 5c/5.10a, in order of descending difficulty.

“Climbing Margarites for the first time I thought that climbing it without a rope was impossible for me,” Taistra shared with Climbing, “and that’s exactly how the plan was born—first get to know the route, and then properly assess my skills.” Taistra says that when she finished free soloing Margarites, she thought: “Oh, that’s it?”

Taistra already put down one of the hardest female free solos in history in May, when she climbed Alfredo Alfredo (5.11d/7a) ropeless. Now, the only known harder female free solo belongs to French legend Catherine Destivelle, who climbed an unnamed route in Mali without a rope that she said maxed out at 7b or 5.12a/b.

In May, 44-year-old Taistra told Climbing that free soloing gives her “so much peace” and feels less stressful than climbing with a rope. The 44-year-old climber rehearses her routes on toprope until she feels confident in the moves.

#8293. The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

As the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other users.

Those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

Don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

Don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

We expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

As trail runners, we move relatively quickly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail users. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

This is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail users.

Greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

If you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy

Don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

In a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more important that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”

So, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

Technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other users, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other users and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

Don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

If running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you plan to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

Trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!

#8292. “We’re Kind of Crushing It.” Why One Wyoming Mountain County Has a Life Expectancy of 94.

According to new data, residents in Wyoming’s Teton County have the highest average life expectancy in the country: 94 years.

Jackson Hole News and Guide first reported the finding on November 4, and Travis Riddell, MD, MPH, the director of the Teton County Health Department, first presented the data point at a Teton County Board of County Commissioners meeting on October 26.

After looking at mortality data over a three-year period, between 2022 and 2024, using U.S. Census population projections for the county as the denominator, Dr. Riddell and experts at the Teton County Health Department found that residents of the county have a life expectancy of 94 years. Dr. Riddell said that beyond comparisons to national averages and Wyoming state averages, they also compared Teton County data to that of 13 other comparable counties with popular mountain towns—called “peer counties”—including Vail in Eagle County, Colorado, Aspen in Pitkin County, Colorado, and Park City, Utah, in Summit County, among others. The numbers will be formally published in Teton County’s Triennial Community Health Assessment in June 2027.

To put the number in perspective, the average life expectancy across the United States is 79 years, per the most recent mortality data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released in 2024.

“My job here as the director of our health department is to encourage and promote health and the health of our community. And to see longevity like that, it almost makes me wonder if I will still have a job moving forward. We’re kind of crushing it, at least in this specific metric,” Dr. Riddell told Outside.

Longevity remains one of the biggest buzzwords in health conversations, with people trying any number of elixirs, fitness tests, or extreme biohacking measures to live longer. But what if living longer is as simple as getting outside and moving your body? And how can people emulate the lifestyle of mountain residents to live a longer, healthier life?

Here’s what Dr. Riddell and Ingrid Yang, MD, an internal medicine physician specializing in longevity and not affiliated with the Teton County Health Department, had to say.

Teton County is the 12th-largest county by total area in Wyoming and has a population of roughly 23,000 people. It’s known for its scenic mountain landscapes and is home to Grand Teton National Park, around 40 percent of Yellowstone National Park, and Jackson Hole—a premier hub for outdoor recreation and winter sports.

Teton County isn’t alone; other mountainous counties also have high life expectancies, according to 2025 data from the Demographics Atlas, which draws on data from the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics. San Miguel County, home to Telluride, Colorado, has a life expectancy of 86.5 years; Summit County, home to Park City, Utah, has a life expectancy of 84 years; and Deschutes County, home to Bend, Oregon, has a life expectancy of 80.9 years.

Life expectancy refers to how long a population in a specific place is expected to live. Because we can’t predict how long people will live, public health experts rely on statistical data to determine average lifespan.

“Life expectancy is a really common metric used to measure health and longevity of various populations. And of course it’s a broad number. It is not necessarily indicative of any one individual’s expected life duration. That all depends on many, many factors, some of which we get to choose in life and others which we do not,” Dr. Riddell said. Those factors may include geographic location, family medical history, access to healthcare and nutritious food, and disease risk, according to Cleveland Clinic.

At nearly 20 percent higher than the national average, Teton County’s 94-year life expectancy is an exceptional statistic. This recent data suggests that mountain towns may be leading the charge in longevity. Why is that?

“That is the million-dollar question for sure,” Dr. Riddell said. Again, any conversation about why a population lives or dies isn’t definitive, so while reasons why the life expectancy is as high as it is are speculative, they are still informed by scientific data.

“We know that Teton County is a really, really healthy place. I think recreation opportunities here are off the charts. We have low smoking rates, we have low obesity rates, and we have low disease rates that are associated with all of those things,” Dr. Riddell said.

But there may be a bit of a chicken-and-egg scenario happening here, too, Dr. Riddell said. Teton County is a healthy place, but its culture of outdoor recreation and healthy living might attract people who already have an affinity for that lifestyle.

There’s a caveat, though. While exercise is largely protective of joints and helps lower chronic inflammation over time, Dr. Yang told Outside, the biggest risk to longevity in the mountains is trauma.

“Ski, bike, and climbing injuries such as anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears damage joints far more than [regular] wear and tear does.” Extreme lifelong endurance training has been linked with higher rates of atrial fibrillation (an irregular heartbeat) in some athletes, Dr. Yang said. This doesn’t negate the overall benefits, though, she explained. Staying active is still a protective measure. “For almost everyone, the danger is too little activity, not too much,” she said.

Other facets of mountain town life, Dr. Yang said, like social connection, proximity to green spaces, and cleaner air, are also associated with long-term health.

Another major factor is wealth. “Teton County is the wealthiest county in the U.S., with one of those measures being per capita income. That brings resources that another county this size might not have,” Dr. Riddell said. He named health delivery services, high-end food options, and restaurants as a few of those beneficial resources.

“In the U.S., income is one of the strongest predictors of how long people live,” Dr. Yang said. “A 2016 study reported that at age 40, the richest one percent outlive the poorest one percent by 14.6 years (men) and 10.1 years (women),” she said.

Dr. Yang said that living at altitude may also play a role in longevity. “Teton County sits at an average elevation of 7,800 feet. At that height, moderate altitude is linked with lower cardiovascular mortality and better metabolic profiles,” she said. Still, Dr. Yang noted that the people who live there and their overall lifestyle outweigh any potential effect of altitude. And very high altitude—above 11,500 feet—Dr. Yang said, is linked with accelerated aging.

To reap the benefits of mountain-town living no matter where you’re based, Dr. Yang suggests keeping the following in mind:

#8289. New Climbing Gym in Massachusetts Plans to Give Away All Its Profits

Berkshire Boulders General Manager Austen McNulty (left) and founder Nick Friedman (right) inside the gym. (Photo: Courtesy Nick Friedman)

The United States has become known for corporate climbing gyms and nationwide chains fraught with labor issues that charge high dollar. A recent analysis by an adventure travel company, which leverages 2026 data as well as the Climbing Business Journal’s 2025 trends report, declared that “the United States is the industry’s laboratory” when it comes to mega-gyms backed by private equity. As climbing becomes more popular, and thus more profitable, one may question whether these gyms will inevitably become the norm.

But in Great Barrington, a small town of a little more than 7,000 residents in Western Massachusetts, entrepreneur Nick Friedman is moving in the opposite direction: starting a new, independent gym that gives away all its profits.

You can trace the 38-year-old’s vision for an altruistic gym back to his childhood, when his dad put his career on hold to demand that General Electric clean up the river that ran through town—and Friedman’s property. In the 1970s, General Electric dumped polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) into the Housatonic River, so Friedman’s dad fought to hold the company liable. GE settled, paying $250 million.

In the process, Friedman learned the importance of activism. The cause close to Friedman’s heart is climbing access, which is not exactly easy to come by in Great Barrington or the Berkshires—but not for a lack of rock. While he calls the climbing in Great Barrington world-class, he says that privately owned land and conservation organizations that don’t understand the value of climbing make access a problem.

“Great Barrington is this unique case study in incredible climbing that is barred from true public domain due to land access challenges,” said Friedman, who has been deeply involved in local access work. In 2023, Friedman, who also serves on the board of the Western Massachusetts Climbers’ Coalition (WMCC), purchased a 70-acre parcel in the Farley Ledges climbing area. This bought WMCC time to organize the permits and funding to purchase it from Friedman earlier this year. While Farley Ledges currently remains closed due to an access issue involving a private landowner, WMCC is raising funds to construct a new parking lot and trail to reopen climbing.

Making these land purchases and forging the agreements necessary to maintain and expand access in Western Massachusetts takes a lot of resources, Friedman explains. That’s where his new gym, Berkshire Boulders, which opens on November 6, comes in. He plans to donate 100% of his profits to community organizations, including WMCC and Access Fund.

“The WMCC is very excited about the opening of Berkshire Boulders and the potential it has to positively impact climbing access in Western Massachusetts,” said Regina Madden, a WMCC board member and chair of its communications committee. Protecting and maintaining access requires ongoing resources, so a local business committed to supporting that mission creates an excellent opportunity. In addition, Berkshire Boulders can serve to bridge the gap between indoor and outdoor climbing, helping to foster a stronger sense of stewardship and community.

While Friedman may pursue nonprofit status down the line, he says it was faster to get the gym off the ground as a business that gave away its profits, rather than a 501(c)3 nonprofit. And as someone who has specialized professionally in startups, he adds that he’s always been “intrigued” by hybrid models that blend for-profit business models with nonprofit values.

Currently, the organizations Berkshire Boulders plans to support include WMCC and Access Fund, as well as non-climbing local organizations including the Railroad Street Youth Project and Greenagers, which fosters sustainability work among youth.

“I felt that a climbing gym could play a central role in that effort and become this anchor and the starting point for a broader vision of bringing outdoor recreation more front and center in this small town,” Friedman said.

Friedman doesn’t see accessibility as a binary, “indoors or outdoors” issue; he views it holistically. This is why he’s made it the gym’s mission to improve climbing access indoors and out. He envisions a gym as a place where you can learn the sport, meet partners, and find people to help you make the gym-to-crag transition. In Friedman’s view, that gym-to-crag transition is the end game. That’s why he decorated Berkshire Boulders’ walls with photographs of Great Barrington rock, and rents out crashpads to climbers who want to try bouldering outside, but lack the gear.

But the other end game is community, which he says is hard to foster when you’re answering to private equity investors. Berkshire Boulders’ KPIs will instead revolve “around community impact.”

One way he’s doing that is by offering hardship memberships. Each month, Berkshire Boulders will award free memberships to low-income individuals through a lottery system. This addresses the known problem of affordability in the gym industry—one so notable that the American Alpine Club declared it an access issue in 2024. Friedman says he’s already approved one hardship membership application, but doesn’t have a monthly quota in mind yet. “We do expect to expand that program significantly over the next several months,” Friedman said.

A focus on community KPIs, however, will not come at the expense of a high-quality bouldering facility. Friedman insists that he is committed to a top-tier facility. He is partnering with local hold-maker Decoy and plans to change the setting across the 15-foot-high walls every two weeks. The gym also features a custom-built, “artistically created” adjustable spray wall. Using the Clift app, climbers will be able to set sequences, replicate local outdoor problems, and track leaderboards.

Currently, for Friedman, Berkshire Boulders is a passion project. His personal endgame is not to make a living off the gym—he still works full-time as the chief strategy officer at a small-batch cannabis startup. He also hired an experienced general manager to run the gym. Rather, that Friedman hopes to ultimately do is drive positive change in his local climbing community.

“Personally, I would love to see the Great Barrington climbing become a published resource for the public,” Friedman said. It’s a long game, but a worthy one, in his view, to turn the local climbing from an underground, tricky access dance to a veritable destination with routes documented on Mountain Project, a guidebook, and formal parking and approach trails.

Beyond local impact, could Berkshire Boulders, if successful, inspire a rising tide of small, mission-driven gyms in this era of indoor climbing corporatization? Friedman believes smaller gyms with a focus on community have a better shot at bringing together passionate climbers than the larger conglomerate gyms. “I would love to see an expansion of smaller independent gyms regionally,” he says.

#8287. 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

After landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

On the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

However, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

We did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

Linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden said, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”

Linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Survival quickly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

One of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling plan was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden said. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”

Assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other plans. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

Next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden said. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”

Pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden said, “the final lap or two is about racing.”

When things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden said. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”

While Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden said. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”

#8286. A Woman Was Swept Off an Oregon Beach and Left Clinging to Rocks Offshore. A Lifeguard Rescued Her in the Darkness.

Rocky sea stacks rise along Oregon’s southern coast, where a woman was swept into the ocean by massive waves at Secret Beach on November 8. (Photo: Juan Pablo Jim/Getty)

A woman was rescued from the ocean after powerful waves swept her off a beach in southern Oregon on November 8, leaving her clinging to rocks offshore as darkness fell.

The woman had been walking along Secret Beach, a secluded stretch of rocky coastline roughly 20 miles north of the California border, when a swell pulled her into the ocean, according to a statement posted to Facebook by Curry County Aquatic Safety. Unable to reach her, the woman’s husband called 911 around 5:18 P.M. The report did not name the woman.

When a Curry County sheriff’s deputy arrived at the scene, the woman had been swept 200 feet down the coastline, where she was stranded on rocks roughly 50 to 70 feet offshore.

“People want to come see the waves, and we have a lot of great scenic viewpoints for them,” Luke Martinez, an aquatic safety officer and lifeguard with Curry County Aquatic Safety, told Outside. “Unfortunately, people sometimes get stuck in bad spots, and that was the case Sunday night.”

The National Weather Service had issued a high surf warning for Oregon’s southern coast that day, forecasting breaking waves of 25 to 33 feet.

Martinez told Outside that he and fellow lifeguard Shannon Ingram responded to the emergency as large waves continued crashing onto the beach.

“It was pretty unruly,” Martinez said. “There was huge surf. The tide was out, and we couldn’t see much, but there were surges occurring up and down the beach.”

Ingram reached the shoreline ahead of Martinez just after sunset. Wearing a wetsuit and a safety helmet, she determined she could safely enter the churning water and made her way to the stranded woman. She checked her for injuries, secured her with a rescue tube, and brought her back to shore.

The woman was able to walk off the beach with assistance before being taken to a hospital for further evaluation.

“It was a good ending to something that could have been pretty bad,” Martinez said.

Secret Beach sits along the Samuel H. Boardman State Scenic Corridor, a 12-mile stretch of coastline dotted with rocky cliffs, secluded beaches, and offshore rock formations. Martinez noted that the area has surged in popularity due to social media, even though its rugged geography poses serious risks.

“We live along a really rugged coastline,” Martinez said. “It’s similar to people visiting the mountains and climbing 14ers. Not everybody realizes the dangers involved.”

Curry County Aquatic Safety has just two lifeguards—Martinez and Ingram—covering roughly 100 miles of coastline and several rivers. On November 8, they spent much of the day advising beachgoers about the unusually powerful surf, emphasizing that volatile conditions can catch people off guard before help can arrive.

“Beachgoers will be watching the smaller waves, thinking they understand how far the water is reaching up the beach,” Martinez explained. “Then that longer-period swell arrives and surges much farther up the beach than the waves they’ve been watching. During these events, our beaches can become dangerous for anybody, including experienced surfers or swimmers.”

Massive waves are a recurring hazard along the Pacific coast from October through March, when winter storms generate the largest swells, according to the state of Oregon. During major storms, offshore waves can exceed 30 feet.

Also on November 8, videos captured similar scenes elsewhere along the coast. Footage from Cannon Beach showed a young girl nearly being swept into the ocean, while another video from Winchester Bay showed two people scrambling to escape incoming waves as their dog was swept into the water. The dog was later rescued.

Another round of massive surf is expected to batter the Oregon coastline in mid-November. A National Weather Service warning projects breaking waves reaching 30 to 35 feet November 13 and 14. The agency is urging visitors to stay off beaches, rocks, jetties, and piers while the high swells continue.

#8284. Watch: Jessie Diggins Explains Why Sparkles Are Her Superpower

Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

On paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

This interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

Jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

Having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really big for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

And then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

And then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

And so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a big thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making new friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

No, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

And so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite quickly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

Now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

Like with any work project, any life thing, I think that a little bit of nerves is super healthy. It also brings out the adrenaline and it tells your body, ‘I am ready to perform.’ But I would get nervous to the point where I’m stealing all my energy, and so it was hard to take yourself too seriously when you’re actually just covered in glitter. And so I would put on the sparkles as this promise to myself, like, ‘Hey, I get to be here. I get to do this. I got to sign up for this. That’s amazing. I have an opportunity to go out there and do my best at a sport that I love with a team that I love, and that’s really cool.’ And so the glitter was my pre-race ritual of ‘I’m going to go out there and have fun and remember to smile at the start because I’m so lucky to get to do this.’ Because sport is ultimately in the entertainment category. It is literally fun and games.

At the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

#8283. How Useful Is An Alpine Climbing Award, Really?

The Ultar Sar team, of Sebastian Pelletti, Ethan Berman, and Maarten Van Haeren, accept their Piolet d'Or in Saint-Christophe-En-Oisans, France, in October 2026. (Photo: Piotr Drożdż)

When I learned I’d be attending a gala for the “Oscars of Alpinism,” I made a note to pack formal clothes. The Piolets d’Or, or Golden Ice Axes, is a big deal; a rare career-building opportunity in a professional alpinist’s life. Earning this award can transform a strong amateur into a full-fledged member of global alpinism’s elite. This year, I joined the recipients who’d been coaxed out of their humble mountain hideouts to partake in alpinism’s biggest award ceremony.

Established in 1992, the Piolets have a respectable mission: to promote difficult, alpine-style new routes on the world’s great mountains. But the award has weathered plenty of criticism over the years. After rejecting his Piolet nomination in 2006, U.K. legend Ian Parnell later wrote in Alpinist: “Is it possible to choose a winner in an inherently unquantifiable pursuit [like alpinism]?” Others decry the Piolets d’Or for awarding climbers who recently died in the mountains, as well as for holding a subjective line of what counts as good climbing style.

I’ve been critical of the Piolets at times myself, especially after hearing one well-known alpinist talk longingly of wanting to climb something worthy of the award. I winced thinking about anyone tackling runout mixed terrain at high altitude with a golden ice axe taunting them overhead.

I thought of these critics, and my own biases, during my transatlantic flight a few weeks ago to this year’s ceremony in Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans, France. The award clearly has a dark side. But it has also become increasingly important in the year 2026. Lately, I’ve watched the professional climbing landscape bend to the pressures of sponsorship and social-media engagement—physical performance is but one metric to make a modern-day alpinist’s career.

In this new landscape, we see some climbers eager to make a quick buck. Others orient ascents around appeasing future sponsors or gaining attention online. In some instances, this materializes as full-scale fraud. In others, imaginative white lies of what constitutes a “summit.”

Through this lens, the Piolets d’Or represents an institution that is slowly becoming necessary. Nearly every year for the last 34 years, a varied, rotating cast of legendary alpinists sifts through the reams of new climbing achievements. Tossing aside marketing fluff and half-baked route attempts, they present to the world the year’s genuine highpoints of alpinism.

I wanted to know: Does the good of the Piolets d’Or outweigh the bad?

The singular Piolet d’Or first launched with the aim of recognizing the greatest alpine ascent of the previous year. In true Oscars’ fashion, at the early Piolet, all of the potential candidates were invited to an in-person ceremony, where the sole winner was read out, for the first time, in front of a couple thousand people.

“It was a mess,” British alpinist Paul Ramsden, one of this year’s jury members, told me of the Piolet’s early days. He and countryman Mick Fowler had been invited to the ceremony in Paris in 2003, when their ascent of Siguniang (6,250m) in China was in the running. “We all got up onto the stage, and they read my and Mick’s names out, and a French team beside us burst into tears,” Ramsden said.

American Dean Potter was on stage too, in the running for his solo ascents of the Patagonian spires Cerro Torre and Fitz Roy. When he got snubbed, he was livid, Ramsden remembered. Potter screamed at the organizers, asking why they’d told him to fly all the way to Europe to stand on stage for an award they knew he’d never receive.

Later that evening, in a sign of the early Piolet d’Or attitude, a special party took place offsite to celebrate Ramsden and Fowler’s win. With his golden ice axe in hand, Ramsden remembered ambling over to the afterparty, only to be stopped by a bouncer. The club had a dress code, and Ramsden was wearing sneakers. “So we weren’t allowed into our own party,” Ramsden laughed.

The Piolet d’Or ran uninterrupted from 1992 to 2007, when mounting criticism came to a head. Most notable was from the Slovenian alpinist Marko Prezelj, who was invited to that year’s event after his ascent of Chomo Lhari (7,326m), on the border of Tibet. He walked slowly onto the stage, took a long pause, then refused to accept his award, explaining why he thought the Piolet was antithetical to his view of alpinism. “Comparing different climbs is not possible without some kind of personal involvement and even then it is difficult,” Prezelj later wrote. “Last year I climbed in Alaska, Patagonia, and Tibet. I cannot decide which expedition was the most… the ‘most what’ in fact?”

Prezelj and others had become increasingly uneasy with how the Piolet d’Or pitted alpinists against each other. With only one winner, everyone else, in their eyes, became a loser. Such was not the spirit of alpinism.

The organizers cancelled the ceremony in 2008 and took a beat to reimagine it. A year later, after personnel changes and plenty of disagreements, a new version of the Piolet emerged, complete with an updated charter. The now-plural Piolets rewarded a climb’s lightweight style, self-sufficiency, technical difficulty, and management of objective hazards. Most importantly, though, the Piolets adopted a more community-based attitude. Everyone who was nominated for the award was given a Piolet d’Or.

This year’s ceremony was devoid of the drama that tainted the Piolet’s past. No one walked onto the stage just to reject the award. There was no French team in tears, and—as far as I could tell—no leery feeling of one-upsmanship among the award recipients. It was a bunch of climbers, wearing sneakers and duct-taped down jackets, drinking a bit too much red wine.

Paul Ramsden, who is 57, has been to a number of these week-long parties over the years, five times as a recipient—the most of any climber—and multiple times again as a jury member. Despite the criticism it’s received over the years, and his own jarring experience in 2003, he is now a proud supporter of the Piolets d’Or.

“I see awful style from climbers in some parts of the world,” he told me, citing large teams with bolt kits and hundreds of meters of fixed ropes, all but assured to succeed with enough dogged, industrial determination. “By rewarding alpine-style climbs, we’re not really rewarding the recipients. We’re signalling to the rest of the climbing community what ‘good’ style is.” In practice, that means that if a climber doesn’t have the skill to scale an unclimbed face with the same hardware they might take to a crag, they should leave the objective for a future generation of climbers who can.

One alpinist, who wished to remain anonymous, but has been nominated for a Piolet before, emphasized how flimsy and subjective any notion of “good” climbing style is. In a phone call with me, they noted how the Piolets jury considers climbing in insulated boots and ultralight crampons with Google-Earth reconnaissance as “good” climbing style, but considered carrying a few extra ropes to fix sections of the route poor form. The jury considers climbing in a lightweight team of two an enviable expression of alpine self sufficiency, yet a team of five or six is antiquated and ungainly.

Even understated, minimalist climbing expeditions to the Himalaya these days require a cottage-industry of resources: international flights, bus rides, porters, cook tents, tens of thousands of dollars of equipment—the list goes on. Deciding what the “correct” amount of resources an expedition should use is an inexact science, and one which the Piolets jury is still figuring out.

“I think it’s cool that we have a pretty objective governing body deciding what is actually good for alpine climbing,” Australian-Argentine climber Sebastian Pelletti, a recipient of a Piolet this year, told me. Like me, Pelletti has noticed professional alpinists erroneously claiming a “new” route to their sponsors and the world.

Last year, I wrote about one of those so-called new routes on Jirishanca (6,094m), in Peru’s Cordillera Huayhuash. Three very famous European alpinists climbed about a thousand meters of new terrain to the mountain’s summit ridge. Above, a spine of unconsolidated snow—the crux of the mountain—proved too difficult for the team. They bailed. A few days later, the climbers and their sponsors plastered a topo for this new route far and wide, drawing a bright red line that stopped on Jirishanca’s “east summit.” The east summit does not exist, nor has it ever been considered a final destination on the mountain. It is a brief bump in an otherwise vertical landscape, at least six pitches below Jirishanca’s actual summit.

When I wrote that article, some people called it a hit piece; I thought I was going light on the climbers. So when the Piolets d’Or announced their “long list” of notable ascents of 2025 earlier this year, I combed through it, seeing which routes made the cut. (Not all long-listed ascents are short-listed for the Piolets d’Or. The long list aims to recognize all new alpine climbs accomplished in good style.)

The Jirishanca “east summit” team was absent in the Peru section; the jury had not even considered their effort a route. But also within Peru’s long list, in the very same Huayhuash range, was a route on a mountain I had not heard much about, by climbers far less famous than their peers down valley. It was about the same length as the Jirishanca route, and just as difficult, but it went to the summit of Yerupajá Grande (6,635 m) and down the opposite side of the mountain. The climbers called it The Essence of Commitment, and they were being awarded the highest prize in alpinism.

#8282. Is an AI Data Center Coming to a National Park Near You? This New Map Shows Where.

(Photo: Courtesy of More Than Just Parks)

As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks.

Will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers. According to his research, at least 14 proposed data center projects are within ten miles of a national park boundary. His data also shows that 38 sites are planned within 25 miles of a national park, and 131 are within 50 miles.

“The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside. “The stance that we take is that we don’t want them on public lands.”

“Places like Utah, for example, have a huge amount of data center projects and some of the biggest ones that are being proposed,” Pattiz said. “Just depending on the size and scale, they take up a massive amount of resources and will have impacts on public lands one way or the other, whether it’s taking water or the land itself.”

Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware.

“The question that we want to see asked is: ‘What is the public benefit from this?’” Pattiz said. “So far, the ones that have been proposed on public lands, there’s no public benefit that’s been outlined.”

To use Pattiz’s map, a user inputs their zip code, and the site shows the closest data center or proposed facility. The site then suggests how the center will affect utility costs, as well as the groups that support the center.

“You can go through that discovery process yourself to decide whether you support [the center] or not, because these are things that are going to impact all of us, and you can decide where you land on that,” Pattiz said.

The map auto-populates as more information becomes available. As of this writing, the tool reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still in the proposal phase. Of those, 77 are located within ten miles of protected land like national parks, wildlife refuges, and wilderness or conservation areas. Roughly half are in the American West.

In Virginia, 97 data centers are proposed, and 12 are within 25 miles of Shenandoah National Park.

At least 25 data centers are proposed in Indiana, according to the map, and eight are located within 25 miles of Indiana Dunes National Park.

The map also includes several construction proposals that are extremely close to iconic National Park Service sites.

Arizona alone has 26 active proposals, with three within 25 miles of a national park. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning to build a $10 billion data center next to Horseshoe Bend, an iconic viewpoint along the Colorado River. The 500-acre parcel was previously protected for outdoor recreation. According to the City of Page, the proposal is undergoing public review and has not yet been formally adopted, but a planning and zoning meeting is scheduled for November 17.

According to Pattiz’s map, the center is also located about five miles from the northeastern edge of Grand Canyon National Park near Lees Ferry.

Just outside of Price, Utah, Pattiz found that a company called Valar Atomics applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for data center buildouts, including permits for hundreds of small nuclear reactors, a fuel plant, and nuclear waste storage.

According to a report published by NPR, the so-called Project Beehive would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces less than half of that on average, NPR reports.

The land is about two hours from both Arches and Canyonlands National Parks.

Located about 40 miles from Zion National Park, Antelope Data Center is slated for development as part of a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt project that will include an on-site natural gas power plant, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. The Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit in June 2026.

Large-scale data center rollouts represent an inflection point in American history, Pattiz said. As construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in American towns and cities.

Pattiz believes that giving Americans transparent, readily available information about where big tech is breaking ground will help them track what developers are building in their backyards.

“At the end of the day, data is data,” he added. “Whether or not there’s a need for these things is a totally separate question from where they’re being built and what impact they’re going to have on you and the places that you love.”

#8281. Six Feet of Snow Trapped 29 People in the Himalayas. Their Survival Came Down to the Details

(Photo: Screenshot via Aquaterra Adventures)

The mountains around Auden’s Col, an 18,010-foot high-altitude pass in India’s Garhwal Himalayas, looked deceptively calm. It was the afternoon of September 25, 2026; the sky was clear, and the 29-member expedition team had reached base camp at approximately 16,400 feet, preparing to cross one of the region’s most challenging passes the next morning.

But within hours, the weather began to change. A fast-moving depression from the Bay of Bengal swept across the Indian subcontinent towards the Himalayas. The Indian government issued a red alert only after the expedition had reached base camp. From the evening of September 25 through September 27, more than six feet of snow fell.

“There was no advance warning, and forecasting services failed to predict the severity of the storm,” Vaibhav Kala, the founder of Aquaterra Adventures, the Indian adventure outfitter that organized the expedition, tells Backpacker. “The team was caught in a very rare, heavy weather event.”

The group included six clients, three guides, and 20 porters. It was led by Jetendra Singh Rana, a mountaineering guide who had crossed the pass nine times over his 22-year guiding career. Aquaterra Adventures helped open this 10-day route to commercial departures nearly two decades ago.

“This is not a casual trek as the route traverses steep slopes, glacier terrain and moraine, to descend onto the heavily crevassed Khatling Glacier,” adds Kala.

Rana stepped out of his tent at midnight on the 25th and saw clouds stacking up over the col that hadn’t been there earlier.

“Something just did not feel right,” he says. At 2 a.m. on September 26, the sky still hadn’t improved, so he made the first critical decision to call off the next morning’s scheduled ascent to Auden’s Col. By 3:30 a.m., snow had started falling.

“No one questioned [Rana’s] decision, and that was the single most important moment during the entire trek that saved our lives,” Preeti and Raj Chauhan, guests from Bangalore, India, say. Had the group left on schedule, they would have been on the face of the col when the snow arrived. By the end of the day, winds had reached around 62 mph, and temperatures had dropped to about -4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 degrees Celsius).

Informed by two decades of guiding experience, Rana’s choice that morning came from a place of pragmatism: “In the mountains, confidence doesn’t mean ignoring danger. It means understanding the situation, trusting your preparation and making responsible decisions,” he says.

By the afternoon of September 26, the group’s small sleeping tents were no longer safe because of the snow that continued to fall. At around 4 p.m., Rana moved everyone into a The North Face 2-Meter Dome Tent, which served as the group’s dining tent.

Through the night, the wind rose to near-blizzard levels, and the team felt the tent’s metal poles straining. For about two hours, they all took turns pressing on the tent poles from the inside to prevent snow from accumulating.

“We are not sure it helped,” Chauhan says. “But it made us feel useful and not panic.”

Another guest, Vikram Badhwar, describes a quieter fear.

“It is tough to be cooped up in a tent for 48 hours, but no one lost their heads,” he says. “We were joking, laughing, talking and, of course, silently praying for our safe homecoming.”

Outside, porters and staff worked through the night with little equipment, shoveling snow off the tent and cutting a perimeter around the base to prevent the rising wall of snow from crushing it.

The only communication available to the team was through a satellite phone, which Aquaterra requires all its guides to carry. Rana used it to report the snow and relay his decision to cancel the ascent. By September 26, they were having pre-scheduled status-update calls every few hours.

That’s when headquarters concluded that the group could not walk back. Kala called the Uttarakhand tourism secretary, who escalated to the Uttarakhand Disaster Management Authority. The additional district magistrate and divisional forest officer also got involved, along with the Civil Aviation Department and the Indian Army. All six agencies collaborated to requisition nine helicopters to rescue 136 stranded trekkers in the valley, including the Aquaterra team.

On the morning of September 27, during an eight-minute phone call, Kala outlined a plan to airlift the entire team. Rana and his staff were instructed to clear a 10-by-10-meter area for a landing pad. The rescue was scheduled for sunrise the following morning.

On September 28, the weather cleared for a brief four-hour window. The crew dismantled their safety dome and used the flat surface underneath as a landing pad. Because of the continuing storm, Kala guided the pilots over base camp using Google Earth Imagery from his office in Delhi.

The first sortie lifted off about 8:45 a.m. with two passengers. “Departure order was set in advance with the guests so there was no scramble for the aircraft,” says Rana. Aquaterra Adventures was the only group that had given the pilots exact coordinates and a prepared landing zone, keeping them on track. By 11 a.m., all 29 hikers were safe.

The first day’s window evacuated 38 people in total from the valley before the weather closed in again. Thankfully, the remaining stranded hikers were evacuated over the next few days with no fatalities.

According to Kala and Rana, this rescue was one of the most successful mountain operations in Uttarakhand in recent years, thanks to an unprecedented coordination between state governments, regional municipalities, and private agencies.

Kala subsequently submitted a detailed report to the Uttarakhand Government documenting the actions of his team, Rana, and other guides and stakeholders, along with lessons for future expeditions. His key takeaways include focusing on small details like packing a central shelter, shovels, portable power banks, spare satellite-phone charging cables, and ensuring trekkers are always prepared to be rescued.

“Our objective was to cross Auden’s Col, but our responsibility was much bigger than reaching a mountain pass,” Rana says. “The mountains will always be there, and there will always be another opportunity to try again. But the safety of every person on an expedition comes first.”

#8280. New Research Finds That Slower Running May Be Good for Your Brain. A Neuroscientist Weighs In.

It’s easy, as a runner, to slip into an all-or-nothing mindset. There may have been times when you’ve caught yourself thinking, “What’s the point of going on a run if I can’t commit to at least 3 miles?” or “If I’m going to run this slow, I might as well walk—or skip it altogether.”

The reality is that something is almost always better than nothing, and running, even very slowly for a short time, can boost your brain and mood.

In Aug. 2026, researchers in Japan set out to discover if very light intensity running would affect the brain, especially the parts that are involved with executive functioning. They weren’t curious about the effect of very light intensity running over time; rather, they wanted to know if a single bout of light intensity running—just one workout—could yield noteworthy brain benefits.

For their study, researchers recruited 24 young and healthy adults, including 13 males and 11 females, with the average ages of 23.38 and 20.55, respectively.

The main experiment included a control (CON) day and a very slow running (SRUN) day, with every participant engaging in both days. For the CON session, participants sat on a chair on an unmoving treadmill for ten minutes.

Before the SRUN session, maximal oxygen uptake (VO2peak) was measured for each participant to determine a very slow run speed that would elicit 35 percent VO2peak. Then, participants ran on the treadmill for ten minutes at their predetermined very slow speeds.

Males averaged 3.39 mph, and females averaged 2.40 mph. While these are easily walking speeds, the researchers observed that participants were able to maintain running form.

Before and immediately after each session, participants completed the following: The Color-Word Stroop task (CWST) to measure inhibitory control and the Two-Dimensional Mood Scale (TDMS) to measure pleasurable moods.

For the CWST task, participants were shown two rows of letters on a monitor and had to determine (by pressing “yes” or “no”) if the color of the letters in the top row matched the color name written in the bottom row.

There were three conditions: Neutral, Congruent, or Incongruent. For the neutral condition, Xs were written on the top row in a particular color, and the name of that color was written in black on the bottom row.

For the congruent condition, the word “red” was written in red in the top row and, in the bottom row, the word red was written in black. The incongruent condition was included to introduce cognitive interference. In that condition, the word in the top row did not match the colors of the letters, but the bottom row still had the name of the upper row letters’ colors written in black.

For each trial, in which either the neutral, congruent, or incongruent condition was displayed, participants would, as quickly as possible, press either “yes” or “no” to report whether or not the color of the letters in the top row matched the color row in the bottom row.

Participants were given three practice sessions to make sure they understood how to perform the task.

So, what does CWST measure? It directly measures something called Stroop interference, which is the difference in reaction time between the incongruent and neutral conditions.

Essentially, Stroop interference is a way to assess executive function, with lower values indicating higher executive functioning. In this study, Stroop interference was lower after participants ran versus the seated control setting.

The TDMS assessed participants’ arousal and pleasure states. Participants were asked to rate the following eight descriptors on a scale from 0 (“I’m not experiencing this at all”) to 5 (“I’m currently feeling this way quite extremely”): energetic, lively, lethargic, listless, relaxed, calm, irritated, and nervous.

The results indicated that immediately following the short and very slow run, participants reported feeling more energized and content than after the control setting.

But what effect does ten minutes of slow running have on brain activity? To examine this, researchers used a non-invasive brain imaging technique called functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). fNIRS measures changes in hemoglobin throughout the brain’s cortex, which corresponds with cortical activity.

For this study, participants wore an fNIRS cap with electrodes while they performed the CWST task, five minutes after running. As hypothesized, very slow running can generate increased activity in multiple subregions of the prefrontal cortex—namely, the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, and the right and left frontopolar areas.

Activation of these brain regions keeps us sharp and functioning well day to day; the prefrontal cortex is involved with executive functions such as managing competing goals, decision-making, reasoning, and self-control.

There was one more variable that the researchers were curious about: head acceleration. Even among smooth runners that glide across the ground, the head moves vertically with each step.

A previous study suggested that this mechanical force may underlie some of the psychological benefits of running by impacting neurotransmitter activity. So, the researchers of the current study sought to explore that more. They found that even the small head acceleration that occurs during very slow running was positively correlated with the amount of post-run pleasure the participants reported.

As is the case with every study, there were a few limitations. First, electrodes (such as on the fNIRS device) can pick up signals other than neural activation, such as skin blood flow. The researchers minimized this potential by carefully designing their protocol and checking if the data made sense. Second, head acceleration is obviously different between seated controls and running conditions, so a third, walking group would enhance future experiments.

Here’s the main takeaway: a single, ten-minute run at a very slow, almost walking pace may be enough to boost short-term cognitive performance and elevate your mood.

Consider what this means if you’re returning to running after an injury or illness. Or, perhaps you’re in a new season of life, and you can’t, realistically, carve out more than a few minutes to move your body. This study encourages all of us to keep running, no matter how fast or far we go.
